entities.name: Evagrius of Antioch
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Evagrius of Antioch, a prominent figure in the tumultuous ecclesiastical landscape of the late 4th century CE, served as the Eustathian claimant to the See of Antioch from 388 until his death in 392 CE. His brief episcopacy marked the final, contentious chapter of the Meletian Schism, a protracted theological and jurisdictional dispute that had rent the Antiochene church for decades. Evagrius's succession to Paulinus, despite an agreement between the two rival factions to not appoint successors, intensified the rift with the Meletian party led by Flavian, prolonging the schism's resolution and drawing the attention of major ecclesiastical powers in Rome and Constantinople.

Elevated to the episcopate by Paulinus on his deathbed in 388 CE, Evagrius's appointment was a direct challenge to the Council of Constantinople's 381 CE decree which had sought to resolve the Antiochene dispute by recognizing Flavian. His ordination was irregular, lacking the customary episcopal consecration by multiple bishops, further delegitimizing his claim in the eyes of many, including Emperor Theodosius I. Despite this, Evagrius garnered the steadfast loyalty of the Eustathian community within Antioch, who viewed him as the legitimate successor to the Nicene tradition, and he maintained communication with Western bishops, notably Pope Siricius, who largely favored the Eustathian line.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Evagrius's brief but controversial episcopacy prolonged a major schism within the early Christian church for four crucial years, delaying unity and influencing the power dynamics between Eastern and Western ecclesiastical authorities. His irregular succession highlighted the complex jurisdictional and theological disputes of the late 4th century.
